title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Physics is about, how to use these notes, and a map of every unit in First Term.

p: Physics is the science that explains how the world works. It tells us why a ball falls, why a car needs fuel to move, why a stone sinks but a ship floats, and how sound and light travel to us. Everything you see around you in Nigeria, from a generator to a mobile phone to the rain on a zinc roof, follows the rules of Physics.

This is the First Term course of SS1 Physics. It follows the Nigerian curriculum scheme of work for SS1 and prepares you for WAEC, NECO and later for JAMB. In this term you will learn how to measure things properly, how to describe movement, and how to calculate things like speed, acceleration and distance.
Each unit is short enough to finish in one sitting. Read it slowly, one section at a time. Look carefully at every picture, because Physics is easier to understand when you can see it.
When you meet a worked example, cover the answer with your hand, try the working yourself, and only then check. This is the best way to get better at calculations.

At the end of every unit there are practice questions. They do not count towards any mark. They are there to help you check that you really understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit and move to the next one.
Keep a notebook and a calculator close by. Copy the formulas into your notebook in your own handwriting, because writing them down helps you remember them.

title: Physical Quantities: Fundamental Quantities and Units
summary: What a physical quantity is, the seven fundamental quantities, their SI units and the instruments used to measure them.

p: A physical quantity is anything about a material or a system that we can measure. Length of a table, mass of a bag of rice, time to boil water and temperature of the room are all physical quantities.
A measurement always has two parts: a number and a unit. When we say a table is 2 metres long, '2' is the number and 'metre' is the unit. A number alone, like '2', tells us nothing. Always give both.
Physical quantities are put into two groups: fundamental quantities and derived quantities.
Fundamental quantities are the basic quantities. They stand on their own and cannot be written in terms of any other quantity. Think of them as the building blocks of Physics.

Scientists around the world agreed to use the same units so that everybody can understand each other. This agreed set is called the SI system (International System of Units). SI comes from the French name Systeme International d'Unites.
There are seven fundamental quantities. In SS1 you will use the first four most often: length, mass, time and temperature.

sections.h: The pictures of common measuring instruments
p: The picture below shows many instruments used in Physics laboratories. Some of them you will meet in this course: the metre rule and vernier callipers for length, the micrometer screw gauge for very small lengths, the stopwatch for time, the thermometer for temperature and the top pan balance for mass. The voltmeter, ammeter and galvanometer are used for electricity, which you will study in later classes.

img.alt: Poster of measuring instruments: micrometer, metre ruler, protractor, vernier callipers, thermometer, stopwatch, voltmeter, ammeter, galvanometer, top pan balance and cathode-ray oscilloscope
img.cap: Common measuring instruments used in Physics.

p: They are independent: you cannot get one of them by combining the others. For example, you cannot get length from mass and time.
Each has a standard SI unit that everybody agrees on.
They are used to build all the other quantities, which are called derived quantities. You will study these in the next unit.

b: Is 'speed' a fundamental quantity? No. Speed is distance divided by time, so it is made from two other quantities. It is a derived quantity.
Is 'time' fundamental? Yes. We cannot write time in terms of any other quantity.

title: Derived Quantities, Dimensions and Changing Units
summary: How derived quantities are made from fundamental ones, what dimensions are, why units matter, and how to convert between units.

p: A derived quantity is made by combining fundamental quantities using multiplication or division. For example, area is length multiplied by length, so its unit is metre multiplied by metre, written m². Velocity is displacement divided by time, so its unit is metre per second, written m/s or ms⁻¹.
Their units are called derived units. Some derived units are so common that they have special names, like the newton for force and the joule for energy.

b: Force = mass x acceleration.
Unit of mass = kg. Unit of acceleration = m/s², which is m s⁻².
So the unit of force = kg x m s⁻² = kg m s⁻². This is given the special name newton (N).
So 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

p: Dimensions show which fundamental quantities a derived quantity is made from. We use capital letters in square brackets: [M] for mass, [L] for length and [T] for time.
To find the dimension of a quantity, write its formula and replace each quantity by its letter. A power tells how many times that quantity appears.

b: Pressure = force / area.
Dimension of force = [M][L][T⁻²]. Dimension of area = [L²].
Pressure = [M][L][T⁻²] / [L²] = [M][L⁻¹][T⁻²].

p: Checking whether an equation is correct. Both sides of a correct equation must have the same dimension.
Working out a relationship between quantities.
Changing units from one system to another.
Standardisation: the same unit is used everywhere in the world, so a kilogram of rice in Lagos is the same as a kilogram of rice in London.
Accuracy: careful measurement reduces mistakes in experiments.
Reproducibility: another person can repeat your experiment and get the same result.
Communication: scientists can share results with each other without confusion.

sections.h: Changing from one unit to another
p: Sometimes the unit given in a question is not the unit you need. You must change it before you calculate. Use prefixes to help you. A prefix is a short word placed before a unit to make it bigger or smaller.

b: Change 100 cm to metres. 1 m = 100 cm, so 100 cm = 100 / 100 = 1 m.
Change 2 hours to seconds. 1 hour = 60 x 60 = 3600 s, so 2 hours = 2 x 3600 = 7200 s.
Change 3.5 km to metres. 1 km = 1000 m, so 3.5 km = 3.5 x 1000 = 3500 m.

activity: Find the dimension of density (mass divided by volume) and of velocity multiplied by time. Then convert your own height from centimetres to metres.

title: Measuring Mass, Weight, Length and Time
summary: Definitions, units and instruments for mass, weight, length and time, with worked examples.

p: Mass is the amount of matter in a body. It is a scalar quantity, which means it has size only and no direction. The SI unit is the kilogram (kg).
Mass is measured with a beam balance, a triple beam balance, an electronic (digital) balance, or a chemical balance when the mass is very small.
Example: a bag of rice has a mass of 25 kg. Your mass is the same on Earth, on the Moon, and in space.

Weight is the force with which the Earth pulls a body towards its centre. Weight is a force, so it is a vector quantity (it has size and direction, and the direction is downwards). The SI unit is the newton (N).
Weight = mass x acceleration due to gravity, or W = mg. On Earth, g = 9.8 m/s² (often taken as 10 m/s² in calculations). Weight is measured with a spring balance or a newton meter.

b: A body has a mass of 5 kg. Find its weight on Earth.
The same body on the Moon, where g = 1.6 m/s², weighs 5 x 1.6 = 8 N. Its mass is still 5 kg.

sections.h: The difference between mass and weight
p: Mass stays the same everywhere. Weight changes from place to place because the pull of gravity is different. That is why astronauts feel light on the Moon but their mass has not changed at all.

p: Length is the distance between two points. It is a scalar quantity. The SI unit is the metre (m). Different instruments are chosen for different jobs.

p: Time is the ongoing sequence of events. It is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is the second (s). We measure time with a clock or a stopwatch. A pendulum clock is often used in experiments.
Conversions: 1 minute = 60 s; 1 hour = 3600 s; 1 day = 86 400 s.

title: Using Instruments Well and Avoiding Errors
summary: Common errors in measurement, how to avoid them, and why careful measurement matters.

p: No measurement is ever perfect. A small difference always exists between the reading we get and the true value. This difference is called an error. A good scientist cannot remove all errors but learns to reduce them.

Parallax error: this happens when you look at a scale from the wrong angle. The reading seems to move when your eye moves. To avoid it, always place your eye directly in front of the mark, at eye level, so that your line of sight is at 90 degrees to the scale.

Zero error: this happens when the instrument does not read zero when it should. For example a ruler whose end is worn away, or a balance that reads 2 g with nothing on it. You must either correct the instrument or add or subtract the zero error from every reading.

Instrumental error: the instrument is faulty or was not made or marked properly (for example a stretched spring in a spring balance). Use well-kept instruments and check them against a known standard.
Human reaction time: when you start and stop a stopwatch by hand, there is a small delay of about 0.2 second. To reduce its effect, time many swings and divide, instead of timing just one.
Take readings at eye level.
Make sure the instrument is clean and in good condition.
Always check for zero error before you start.
Repeat each measurement at least three times and take the average.
Write the unit with every reading.

b: A pendulum is timed for 20 complete swings and the stopwatch shows 36.0 s.
Time for one swing = 36.0 / 20 = 1.8 s.
The 0.2 s reaction delay is now shared over 20 swings, so its effect on one swing is only 0.01 s.

p: Measurement gives science its accuracy and lets us compare and predict things. It is used every day in industry, engineering, building, medicine and farming: a nurse measures the dose of a drug, an engineer measures the length of a steel beam, and a baker measures the mass of flour. Accuracy and correct use of instruments give reliable results in any experiment.

activity: Use a ruler to measure the width of your desk three times, once with your eye directly above the mark, once from the left and once from the right. Compare the readings and explain what you notice.

title: Position, Distance and Displacement
summary: The meaning of position, distance and displacement, how they differ, and how to calculate each one.

p: Position is where an object is, compared with a fixed point called the reference point or origin. We usually say how far it is from the origin and in which direction (left or right, north or south).
Example: a student sitting 2 m to the right of the board is at position +2 m. A student sitting 2 m to the left of the board is at position -2 m.

Distance is the total length of the path an object travels, no matter which direction it goes. Distance is a scalar quantity, which means it has size only. It is always positive and its unit is the metre (m).
Example 1: you walk 4 m forward and then 4 m back. The total distance = 4 + 4 = 8 m.
Example 2: you walk 6 m east and then 4 m west. The total distance = 6 + 4 = 10 m.

Displacement is the straight line from the starting point to the finishing point, together with its direction. It tells you how far out of place you are and in which direction. Displacement is a vector quantity: it has size and direction. It can be positive, negative or zero. Its unit is also the metre.
Example: you walk 4 m forward and 4 m back. You are back where you started, so your displacement is 0 m, even though you walked 8 m.
A good way to remember: distance is how much ground you covered, displacement is how far you are from the start.

p: Look at each example, then try it again without looking.

b: A boy walks 6 m east and then 3 m west. Total distance = 6 + 3 = 9 m. Displacement = 6 - 3 = 3 m east.
A girl walks 10 m north and then 10 m south. Distance = 10 + 10 = 20 m. Displacement = 0 m, because she is back at the start.
An athlete runs once round a circular track of radius 70 m. Distance = circumference = 2πr = 2 x 3.142 x 70 = 439.88 m. Displacement = 0 m, because the athlete finishes at the start.

p: In a 400 m race on a round track, the distance run is 400 m but the displacement after one full lap is zero.
A car's odometer shows distance travelled. A GPS shows displacement, because it shows where you are compared with where you started.
Pilots and ship captains must use displacement, because they need to know direction as well as distance.

title: Showing Movement on Graphs and Number Lines
summary: How to read position-time and distance-time graphs, how to use a number line, and how to find the size and direction of a displacement.

sections.h: Graphs of position, displacement and distance
p: A graph is a picture of movement. For a position-time graph, time is on the horizontal axis (x-axis) and position is on the vertical axis (y-axis). Read the shape of the line like a story:

A flat horizontal line means the object is not moving (it is stationary). A line sloping upwards means it is moving away from the origin. A line sloping downwards means it is moving towards the origin. The steeper the line, the faster the movement. The slope of the line tells you the velocity.
A displacement-time graph looks the same, but it shows displacement (change in position with direction). Its slope is the velocity.
A distance-time graph shows only the total ground covered, so it never goes downwards. Its slope is the speed.
The picture shows three position-time graphs: a stationary object (flat line), an object moving at uniform speed (straight sloping line) and an object whose speed is changing (a curve).

img.alt: Three graphs of distance against time: a horizontal line for a stationary object, a straight sloping line for uniform speed and a curve for non-uniform speed
img.cap: Stationary object, uniform speed and non-uniform speed.

p: Draw a straight line. Mark 0 as the origin. Put positive numbers to the right and negative numbers to the left. Now you can show position and displacement clearly.
A student walks from 0 to +5 m: distance = 5 m and displacement = +5 m. She then walks back to 0: total distance = 10 m and displacement = 0 m.
Remember that distance graphs do not show direction.

sections.h: When the movement is at a right angle
p: Sometimes a body moves in two directions that are at right angles, for example 100 km north and then 60 km east. The displacement is the straight line from start to finish. Use Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to find its size and direction.

b: A motorist travels 100 km due north and then 60 km due east.
Direction: tan θ = 60 / 100 = 0.6, so θ = 31 degrees. The motorist is 116.6 km from the start, 31 degrees east of north.
Total distance travelled = 100 + 60 = 160 km. Notice that distance (160 km) and displacement (116.6 km) are different.

p: Work through these and check your answer in the practice questions.

b: If a body moves from A to B and back to A in 20 s, covering 40 m in total, its displacement is 0 m and its average speed = total distance / total time = 40 / 20 = 2 m/s.

A student walks round a field 40 m long and 30 m wide. One full lap = 40 + 30 + 40 + 30 = 140 m. The displacement after a full lap is 0. From one corner to the opposite corner the displacement is √(40² + 30²) = √2500 = 50 m.
